questions.text:
Data projectors in classrooms use a concave lens as part of their projection system.

One such projector has an object which is 15 cm from a concave lens with focal length 10 cm.

Draw and label the image in the diagram below.
questions.expectedAnswer: Image found between F and the lens, on the same side

questions.text:
Calculate the magnification of the image.

(Object distance = 15 cm, focal length = −10 cm for concave lens)
questions.markingGuide: 1/f = 1/dᵢ + 1/dₒ. 1/(−10) = 1/dᵢ + 1/15. dᵢ = −6 cm. Magnification = dᵢ/dₒ = 6/15 = 0.4 times. Achieved: Uses f = 10 to get dᵢ = 30. OR correctly identifies f = −10. OR correct description. Merit: Correct magnification. OR made one error overall and has correct description.

questions.text: Fully describe the nature of the image formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Image will be virtual, upright, and diminished.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct description. Excellence: Correct magnification and description.

questions.text:
In another projector, a convex lens is used, and a real image twice as big as the object is formed.

Complete a ray diagram on the grid below to show how the real image that is twice as big as the object is formed.

You must show any calculations you used to decide where to place the object.

Make the object 6 squares tall.
questions.expectedAnswer: dᵢ/dₒ = 2, so dᵢ = 2dₒ. Using 1/f: dₒ = 1.5f OR dₒ = 6 squares. hᵢ = 12 squares.
questions.markingGuide: dᵢ/dₒ = 2 → dᵢ = 2dₒ and hᵢ = 2hₒ. 1/f = 1/dᵢ + 1/dₒ → dₒ = 1.5f OR dₒ = 6 (squares). Achieved: States that dᵢ = 2dₒ. OR hᵢ = 2hₒ OR hᵢ = 12 (squares). Merit: Places object and image so that dᵢ = 2dₒ and hᵢ = 12. AND draws at least one correct ray from object. Excellence: Object and image placed correctly, of the correct size with two correct rays drawn and some evidence of a calculation. E.g. dₒ = 2dᵢ, etc.

questions.text:
An ultra-short-throw projector shortens the projection distance, and still produces high-quality images by using a concave mirror that reflects the light and focuses on the screen.

Complete the ray diagram below to find and draw the image.
questions.expectedAnswer: Image located using two rays. Image is virtual, upright, and enlarged.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct diagram (2 rays). OR correct description. Merit: Correct diagram (2 rays) AND correct description.

questions.text: Describe the nature of the image formed by the concave mirror.
questions.expectedAnswer: Image is virtual, upright, and enlarged.

questions.text:
A double-glazed window has two glass panes with a refractive index of 1.5, separated by an air gap. Matiu notices that a red laser shone through the window does not travel straight through.

On the diagram below, show the path of the ray of light as it crosses from one glass pane to the air.
questions.expectedAnswer: Draws arrow in the correct direction (away from the normal) with arrow head.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Draws arrow in the correct direction (away from normal) with arrow head.

questions.text: Explain what a refractive index of 1.5 means, in terms of the speed of light in the glass.
questions.expectedAnswer: The speed of light is 1.5 times slower in glass than in air.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: The speed of light is slower in glass. OR the speed of light is faster in air than glass. Merit: n_air = 1.5 × v_glass. v_glass = (2/3) v_air. (Accept v_glass = 1/(1.5) × v_air. OR v_glass = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.) Quantitative answer.

questions.text:
Red laser with wavelength 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m enters a different window at an incident angle of 30°. The wavelength of the red light in the glass is 4.64 × 10⁻⁷ m.

Calculate the angle of refraction as the red laser passes from air (n = 1.0) into the glass.
questions.markingGuide: n_glass = λ_air/λ_glass = 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ / 4.64 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.40 (accept 1.4). n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. 1 × sin 30 = 1.40 × sin θ₂. 0.7138 = sin θ₂/0.5. θ_glass = 20.9° ≈ 21°. Achieved: Correct formula identified. OR n_glass = 1.4. OR correct λ_air/λ_glass ratio. Merit: Calculation with ONE error (e.g. θ_glass = 44.4). Excellence: Full calculation with correct angle.

questions.text:
Matiu notices that if he keeps increasing the angle, the ray of light bounces off the inner surface of the glass, and none enters the air.

Name the phenomenon that is occurring.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies TIR. OR ONE of the bullet points about the conditions of TIR.

questions.text:
Describe the conditions needed for this phenomenon to occur.

Calculations are not needed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Light must travel from a medium of higher refractive index to lower
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies TIR. OR ONE of the bullet points about TIR conditions. Merit: Identifies TIR AND partial explanation. Excellence: Full explanation.

questions.text:
Wireless internet connections (Wi-Fi) work by sending information as electromagnetic waves through the air.

What type of wave is an electromagnetic wave?

Wi-Fi interference can be an issue in a populated school environment. This occurs when two or more Wi-Fi access points are using the same channel or frequency, causing interference and reducing the reliability of the Wi-Fi.

Explain how having two Wi-Fi access points emitting waves of the same frequency can cause both spots of strong Wi-Fi signal and spots of weak Wi-Fi signal.
questions.expectedAnswer: When two waves of the same frequency are in the same place, they interfere
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Recognises interference. OR partial answer. Merit: Partial answer. Excellence: Full explanation in the context of signal strength, with path difference in terms of λ (could be correctly labelled diagram).

questions.text:
Internet satellites orbit the Earth at a height of 550 km. The wavelength of the radio wave is 0.025 m.

How many radio waves reach the Earth in 2 hours?
questions.markingGuide: f = v/λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 0.025 = 1.2 × 10¹⁰ Hz. Two hours = 2 × 60 × 60 = 7200 s. Number of radio waves = 1.2 × 10¹⁰ × 7200 = 8.64 × 10¹³. Achieved: Correct frequency. OR calculated t = 7200 s. Merit: Correct answer.

questions.text:
When Wi-Fi signals pass through walls, they slow down. The boundary between wall and air can be modelled by ropes of different densities joined together.

The diagram below models two pulses from two Wi-Fi points travelling towards each other. The speed in air is 2 squares per second, and the speed in the wall is 1 square per second.

Describe how the frequency of the Wi-Fi signal changes as it moves from air to wall.
questions.expectedAnswer: The frequency of the Wi-Fi signal does not change as it enters / leaves the wall from / to the air.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: The frequency is unchanged. OR the correct position of one of the pulses after 3 s. Merit: Same frequency AND one resulting pulse form in the correct place.

questions.text: Assuming any pulse is half the height of the original after it transmits and reflects with the boundary, draw the result of the two pulses' interactions after 3 seconds.
questions.expectedAnswer: Correct diagram showing pulses and frequency unchanged (allow for a minor error).
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: The frequency is unchanged. OR the correct position of one of the pulses after 3 s. Merit: Same frequency AND one resulting pulse form in the correct place. Excellence: Correct diagram showing pulses and frequency is unchanged (allow for a minor error).
